summary: 60 findings: 7 high, 30 medium, 23 low. High: item arthur-parameters' 'equivalently' clause is false for even special orthogonal groups (no discriminant condition; odd-dimensional summands excluded), following a loose sentence of p. 753; route 3 puts Theorem 5.1 = B.2 and its inputs into AS.2, which is upstream of the ML.4 and ET.6 layers they need, a stage cycle; the Bessel data and coefficients are planned by both new roadmaps; the GGP design job is placed in import cycles with its consumers; for unitary groups the paper's complex conjugations are inconsistent (Theorem 5.3's bilinear pairing against Theorem 6.6 and the proofs of Theorems 6.10 and 7.1), which the extraction's period items and E26 resolve one way without checking the rest; item thm-5-7 still states the conclusion that the extraction's own E26 says is unproved; and conj-6-8 drops the standing hypothesis L(1/2, φ × φ′) ≠ 0, without which it is false. Medium findings are wrong statuses and owners (llc-gln's archimedean case, ML.4 for non-quasi-split groups, the ∧²/Sym²/Asai L-functions, the Gindikin–Karpelevich constant term, the unitary duals, the built Witt theory), misstated items (the unitary stabilizer, generic local parameters, the Eisenstein series data, the unitary local L-factor, Proposition 5.4, ψ_{τ,σ}'s parity), missing cited inputs and items (Proposition 2.6's converse, GRS11 and JZ14 for the open cell, the composite non-vanishing, the global Vogan packet), and source gaps in Lemma 6.5, Proposition 6.3 and E4/E5. Low findings are unrecorded misprints, locators, references, notes and the report's wording.

findings.claim: For unitary groups the paper's complex conjugations are inconsistent, and the review fixed one reading (bilinear periods, E26) without checking it against the rest of the paper. Theorem 5.3 as printed pairs pi bilinearly with the descent: <phi_pi, conj F(E)> = integral of phi_pi times F(E) ((4.9) fixes <a,b> = integral of a times conj b). But the paper also asserts F^{O_kappa0}(E_{tau x sigma}) is isomorphic to pi (Conjecture 6.7, Section 7.2, Theorem 7.1). If F(E) is isomorphic to pi then that bilinear pairing vanishes for every vector whenever pi is not isomorphic to conj pi (= pi dual), which happens for unitary groups whenever tau is not self-dual. So for unitary groups the printed Theorem 5.3 and Theorem 7.1/Conjecture 6.7 cannot both hold, whatever the base-change normalization. Concrete instance, U(1) x U(0) (n = 1, l* = 0, kappa* = 0, H_{a+m} = U(1,1), F = restriction to the stabilizer U(1) of w*): take pi = chi with chi^2 != 1 and tau = mu, mu(t) = chi(t/tbar) (standard base change). The residue E_tau is chi'(det) with chi'(t/tbar) = mu(t), so chi' = chi and F(E_tau) = pi (Conjecture 6.7 holds). Then the printed left side is the integral of chi^2 over [U(1)], which is 0, while the right side is phi_pi(1), which is non-zero, so the printed Theorem 5.3 fails. The unbarred (Hermitian) statement <chi, chi> != 0 holds. With the opposite base-change normalization the printed 5.3 holds but F(E_tau) = chi^{-1} is not pi, so Theorem 7.1 fails instead. Hence E26 depends on the normalization. In the standard one, Theorem 5.3 must be Hermitian, and L(s, tau x sigma) in (5.2) is L(s, tau x phi_sigma^vee) (finding 3). Theorem 5.7 then follows as printed for its unbarred hypothesis, and that is GGP for the bilinear pair (pi, conj sigma). E26's replacement by L(s, tau x sigma^vee) would then be the wrong central value. Also: For unitary groups, Theorem 5.3 as printed (bilinear pairing of pi with F(E_{tau x sigma'})) and Theorem 6.6 (every summand of F(E_{tau x sigma'}) has parameter phi_tau) cannot both hold, and the proofs of Theorems 7.1 and 6.10 each use a different one of the two conventions. A summand pi_i of the L^2-subspace F(E) makes the sesquilinear <phi_{pi_i}, F(E)> non-zero; the bilinear <phi_{pi_i}, conj F(E)> = integral of phi_{pi_i} F(E) is non-zero iff the complex conjugate of pi_i, i.e. pi_i^vee, occurs in F(E). By Lemma 6.5 the Satake parameters of pi_i^vee are those of tau^vee = tau^c, so Theorem 5.3 (<=) for pi with parameter phi_tau together with Theorem 6.6 forces tau = tau^vee, false in general for unitary groups (e.g. BC of a U(1)-character eta is z -> eta(z/zbar), not self-dual unless eta^2 = 1). The proof of Theorem 7.1 applies Theorem 5.3 to the summands pi_i using the bilinear pairing; the proof of Theorem 6.10 calls the sesquilinear <phi_pi, F(E(., s))> 'the global zeta integral', whereas (4.9) defines it with the bar. E26 records the conjugation problem only for Theorem 5.7. Orthogonal groups are unaffected (pi^vee is pi or its O~-conjugate, and F(E) is O~-stable by Proposition 6.4). Also: In Section 4 'the Bessel period for (π, σ′)' (and for (σ, π)) is the bilinear pairing defined on p. 776 (and the bilinear inner integral of (4.44)-(4.45)), but these items do not say so, while the extraction's bessel-periods item fixes 'the Bessel period for (π, σ)' to mean the sesquilinear ⟨F(φ_π), φ_σ⟩ = ∫ F(φ_π) φ̄_σ, i.e. the bilinear period of (π, σ^∨). Read with that convention the items are false for unitary groups (where σ′ = σ): Corollary 4.4 would say that vanishing of the (π, σ^∨)-period forces Z ≡ 0, whereas by Proposition 4.3 Z is controlled by the (π, σ)-period; non-vanishing of the two is governed by different central values (the review's own E26 example: L(½, χμ) against L(½, χμ⁻¹)). Also: The item says the Bessel period 'in Conjecture 2.3, (5.6) and Theorems 5.3, 5.7 and 6.10 is the sesquilinear <F(phi_pi), phi_sigma>_H' and that '(5.6) nevertheless writes it P(phi_pi, phi_sigma)'. On the page images, (5.6) and Theorem 5.3 print <F(phi_pi), conj(phi_sigma)>, the bilinear period, consistent with (4.7); the item thm-5-3 (items/44) says so correctly, so the two items contradict each other. The correct split, needed to read thm-6-10 and thm-7-1: sesquilinear (no bar): Conjecture 2.3 (p. 757), Theorem 5.7 (p. 791), Theorem 6.10 (p. 805), Corollary 6.11 (p. 807); bilinear (bar): (5.6) (p. 785), Theorem 5.3 (p. 786), Section 6.2 (p. 801), proof of Theorem 7.1 (pp. 807-808). In particular the sigma of Theorem 7.1 (bar) is the complex conjugate of the sigma that Conjecture 2.3 (no bar) supplies.

The review flagged this in the note ('it should fix one convention') but the statement was not changed. For unitary groups the sesquilinear period of (π, σ) is the bilinear period of (π, σ^∨), and σ^∨ has parameter (φ′)^∨. So by GGP the stated condition is equivalent to L(1/2, φ × (φ′)^∨) ≠ 0, not to L(1/2, φ × φ′) ≠ 0; the two differ (for GL_1 factors, anticyclotomic χ against χ^{-1}). As written, the item is not [GGP12, Conj. 24.1] for unitary groups. It also contradicts its own route 1 brief, which uses the bilinear period ∫ F^{ψ_{ℓ,w_0}}(φ_1) φ_2. Also: global-ggp is attributed to [GGP12, Conj. 24.1, 26.1], but it pairs the paper's sesquilinear period ⟨F^{ψ_{O_ℓ}}(φ_π), φ_σ⟩ = ∫ F(φ_π) φ̄_σ, a bilinear period of (π, σ^∨), with GGP's L-value L(½, φ × φ′). The paper itself identifies the denominator of (4.47) with that normalizing factor (p. 780 and (5.4)). Under that convention the unitary form of (4.47) is L(s + ½, τ_ν × π_ν) / (L(s + 1, τ_ν × σ_ν^∨) L(2s + 1, τ_ν, As^{(−1)^𝔪})). The printed formula is not consistent under any single base-change convention: the alternative convention moves the contragredient to the numerator. Orthogonal groups are unaffected, since σ and σ^∨ have O_𝔪(ℂ)-conjugate parameters.
findings.evidence: Check at a split place ν of E/F for U(3) ⊃ E^× × U(1), τ_ν = (χ_1, χ_2), σ = μ, with BC(μ)(z) = μ(z/z̄) = (μ, μ⁻¹) and the Levi element diag(z, u, z̄⁻¹) ↦ diag(z_1, u_1, z_2⁻¹) ∈ GL_3(F_ν). The Gindikin–Karpelevich factor of the long intertwining operator is L(s, χ_1μ⁻¹) L(s, χ_2μ) L(2s, χ_1χ_2). That is L(s, τ × BC(σ)^∨) L(2s, τ, As), not L(s, τ × BC(σ)) = L(s, χ_1μ) L(s, χ_2μ⁻¹). Paper: p. 780, the ramified factor may be taken 'from the normalization of the local intertwining operators from the Eisenstein series in the global zeta integrals'. (5.4), p. 783, uses the same L_ν(1+s, τ × σ). p. 787 says L(s, τ × π) and L(s, τ × σ) 'are defined in terms of the global Arthur parameters of π and σ'. Cross-check in the atlas: PAPER-BEUZARTPLESSIS-CHAUDOUARD-25 item 58 (Prop. 8.7.2.1), for the same Eisenstein series on U_n induced from τ ⊠ σ_m, has L(½ + s, τ × σ_{n+1}) / (L(1 + s, τ^c × σ_m) L(1 + 2s, τ, As^{(−1)^m})). findings.claim: Item 13 defines L(s, tau x pi) := L(s, tau x phi_pi) and L(s, tau x sigma) as Rankin-Selberg L-functions of general linear groups. For unitary groups this convention makes Proposition 5.4's key claim false. Item 45 records that claim: L(s, tau, pi, sigma; rho) has a pole of order r at 1/2 coming from L(s + 1/2, tau x pi). With phi_pi = phi_tau, L(s, tau x phi_tau) is the product of the L(s, tau_i x tau_j), which has a pole at s = 1 only for pairs with tau_j isomorphic to tau_i^vee = tau_i^c. Counterexample: r = a = 1 and tau = mu, a Hecke character of A_E^x/E^x with mu^c = mu^{-1} and mu^2 != 1. Then L(s, mu x mu) = L(s, mu^2) is entire, so the pole of order r and with it Theorem 5.3 (<=) fail. Likewise the L-function in the constant term (5.2), which items 39 and 42 write as L(s, tau x sigma), is the Rankin-Selberg L-function of tau against phi_sigma^vee, not against phi_sigma. The paper's own proof of Proposition 5.2 writes the cross terms with the conjugate: L(2s, tau_i x tau_j^iota).
findings.evidence: p. 788, proof of Proposition 5.4: 'L(s + 1/2, tau x pi) = prod L(s + 1/2, tau_i x pi) has a pole at s = 1/2 of order r, since the cuspidal automorphic representation pi has the generic global Arthur parameter phi_tau'. p. 783: 'L(2s, tau, rho) = prod L(2s, tau_j, rho) prod_{i<j} L(2s, tau_i x tau_j^iota)'. findings.claim: Theorem 5.1 = B.2 claims that N(omega_0, tau x sigma, s) is holomorphic AND non-zero for Re(s) >= 1/2. For non-generic sigma the proof only shows that each rank-one factor (B.7)-(B.9) is holomorphic and non-zero, and then concludes for the composition. A composition of non-zero operators can be zero. Rank-one normalized operators in this range need not be injective: GL_1 x GL_1 with tau = tau' = 1 at exponent 1 is non-zero with kernel the Steinberg representation. Exponent 1 is reached in (B.7) at s = 1/2 when alpha_j + beta_i = 1/2, which the bounds (B.5)-(B.6) allow. Type (B.9) has reducibility points with s - alpha_j in (0, 1). So non-vanishing is not proved. Only holomorphy is used in Section 5's main chain (Proposition 5.4, the 'only if' half of Proposition 5.2 in Section 5.5). Non-vanishing at s = 1/2 is needed for the 'if' half of Proposition 5.2 (L(1/2, tau x sigma) != 0 implies E_{tau x sigma} != 0), which Section 6.3 uses. Neither item 41 nor any sourceIssue records the gap. Also: The proof of Theorem B.2 (the non-generic case) shows that each rank-one factor (B.7)-(B.9) is holomorphic and non-zero. It then concludes 'Putting together the results for all three types' that the composite N(ω0, τν ⊗ σν, s) is non-zero. This does not follow, because a composition of non-zero operators can vanish. The rank-one factors are in general not injective in the range. Example: for the Levi GL_1 × SO_1 of SO_3 ≅ PGL_2, the operator at exponent s − α_j = 1 (reached for s = 1 + α_j ≥ ½) kills the Steinberg subrepresentation of the reducible Ind(|·|). CKPSS04 needs a separate input at exactly this step, Zhang's lemma (holomorphy implies non-vanishing). The non-vanishing is used: Proposition 5.2's 'pole of order exactly r if and only if L(½, τ × σ) ≠ 0' needs N(ω0, ·, ½) ≠ 0.

findings.claim: For unitary groups the proof of Lemma 6.5 (and the parallel sentence in the proof of Proposition 6.2) only treats places of F inert in E. It asserts that tau_nu is 'completely determined by [a/2] unramified characters', that omega_{tau,nu} 'is a quadratic character - that is, omega_{tau,nu} = 1 or lambda_0', and in Case (2) (H_m quasi-split even unitary, a odd) that omega_{tau,nu} = 1 and that the descent is Ind mu_1 x ... x 1 with 1 'the trivial character of U_1(F_nu)'. At a place nu split in E, E_nu^x = F_nu^x x F_nu^x, U_1(F_nu) = F_nu^x, and the central character of the conjugate self-dual tau_nu is (chi, chi^{-1}) with chi an arbitrary unramified character, so these claims fail (a = 1: tau a conjugate-orthogonal Hecke character of infinite order). Split places cannot be dropped: Lemma 6.5 is used at almost all places to identify the global parameter of the summands in Theorem 6.6(2), and places of E over inert places have Dirichlet density 0 and do not distinguish tau from its conjugate tau^c = tau^vee (an unramified character chi_w of E_w^x, w inert, is fixed by Galois conjugation, so chi and chi^c = chi^{-1} have the same local components at all inert places). So for G_n = U_{2n+1} the proof does not establish that the descent has parameter phi_tau rather than phi_{tau^c}; the statement is plausible (the split-place computation is a GL_{2a+m_frak} computation) but unproved in the paper.

Denote omega_{tau,nu} to be the central character of tau_nu. Since tau_nu is (conjugate) self-dual, omega_{tau,nu} is a quadratic character - that is, omega_{tau,nu} = 1 or lambda_0. Here lambda_0 is the unique non-trivial unramified quadratic character of E_nu^x.' p. 799: 'suppose that H_m is quasi-split even unitary. Then in our setting a is odd, tau_nu is conjugate orthogonal and omega_{tau,nu} = 1 ... (6.6) F(Sigma_nu) < Ind mu_1 x mu_2 ... x mu_{[a/2]-1} x 1, where 1 is the trivial character of U_1(F_nu).' p. 800: 'Therefore, we complete all cases involved in our discussion in this paper'.
